https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Andy Burnham said he was proud to roll out a measure he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester across the country as a whole Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham said he was proud to roll out a measure he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester across the country as a whole Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty Images Transport policy Burnham scraps restrictions on disabled people’s bus passes in England Move means holders will be able to travel free on local services at any time of day or night from April next year Aletha Adu Political correspondent Mon 17 Aug 2026 17.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Disabled people across England will be able to use their free bus passes at any time of day from next April, as Andy Burnham expands a policy he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester. The prime minister has said the current weekday restrictions on when disabled people can use their bus passes will be removed from 1 April 2027. Their passes are valid only between 9.30am and 11pm on weekdays, although some councils pay to allow people free travel outside those hours. The change means disabled bus pass holders will be able to travel free on local bus services where the pass applies at any time of day or night. The charity Mencap welcomed the measures, noting that disabled people often struggle with the cost of living as well as the cost of their disability. Burnham is putting up £60m in funding for the change, with £40m coming from the Department for Work and Pensions and £20m from the Department for Transport . Government sources said the funding has no set end date and was not a one-off payment. They said the change would take seven months to introduce because it must be passed by parliament, and the April start date gave local transport authorities time to prepare. Burnham is on the second week of his summer tour during which he is focusing on the cost of living. The disabled bus pass policy has been in place in Greater Manchester since March. “Buses are a lifeline for so many people – making it easier to get to work, education and healthcare,” Burnham said. “It’s simply not right that many disabled people cannot travel using their pass during certain times of the day. So we’re fixing that. Disabled people will now have unlimited free bus travel 24/7. “I did it before in Greater Manchester and I’m proud to do it now for the whole country. This is part of our ongoing action to bring back hope and give people some much needed breathing space on the cost of living.” Ministers say the move will help disabled people get into work, education and training as well as helping with the cost of living. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the change would end a postcode lottery under which disabled people got different levels of support depending on where they lived. The government says the measure is part of wider plans to make bus travel cheaper, including keeping the £2 fare cap throughout 2027 and giving under-16s free bus travel this summer. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The executive director of strategy impact and social change at Scope, James Taylor, said: “Disabled people face extra costs every day and many need to travel in the morning for work, education and healthcare. Making free bus travel available around the clock is a welcome step that will put money back in people’s pockets and remove barriers to everyday life.” The chief executive of Bus Users UK, Lydia Horbury, said: “Disabled people don’t live off-peak lives. Lifting these restrictions nationwide replaces an arbitrary postcode lottery with genuine freedom, independence and dignity. “It will help more disabled people access work, reduce isolation, support bus use and reduce unnecessary car dependency.” Explore more on these topics Transport policy Bus fares Consumer affairs Labour Road transport Transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: 1:28 Police clash with students and workers protesting in Paris – video France More than 400 arrested as police clash with protesters across France Police fire teargas in Paris and protesters storm town hall in Marseille – with officials blaming violence on ‘ultra-left’ Kim Willsher in Paris and William Christou Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.15 EDT First published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 400 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school student grievances clashed with police. Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry over high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across the country, and tensions erupted on the fringes of the nationwide demonstrations over absent teachers, decrepit school buildings and police violence. Late on Saturday, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been 400 arrests and most were adults and not part of the high school protests. He said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “ opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”. He said the state was not planning to declare a state of emergency but added: “I very strongly condemn the violence we have seen.” In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall, ramming the door with security barriers they removed from the street. They briefly managed to enter the municipal building, where a protester spray-painted an “A” for anarchy on a wall before the police removed them. View image in fullscreen A masked protester holds the French flag as he stands on the statue of the Place de la République. Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters Around Place de la République in central Paris , a peaceful march turned violent, with police firing teargas at black-clad and masked rioters who threw fireworks and paving stones, attacked a bank and looted a sports shop. “We’re taking the Bastille!” one demonstrator yelled. Others set wheelie bins on fire and threw firecrackers inside or pushed over glass recycling bins and picked up the bottles inside to use as missiles. A lorry was set on fire and flames spread to a nearby building. Along Boulevard Magenta, one of the main south-north axis north of Place de la République running through a mostly working-class area, dozens of shops were broken into and looted. Residents in surrounding streets were forced to close windows and doors as huge clouds of teargas rose to roof level. French authorities detained dozens of protesters across the country, with more arrests expected. Saturday’s mobilisation followed calls on social media to revive the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris , where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards. Saturday’s protests called for teachers and students, labourers, pensioners and farmers to join the protests and widen the movement. Map French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday, blaming the unrest and violence on what they said was the “ultra-left”. View image in fullscreen French riot police detain a protester in Marseille. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images The CGT, one of France’s biggest labour unions, has also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”. About 45% of French people are worried about the rising cost of living and inflation, according to a 2,000-person survey conducted in October. Protesters ⁠in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, and in Marseille rubbish bins were set ​alight. Both the far left and far right in France sought to capitalise on the protest movement, with the left positioning itself on the side of the protesters and the right backing the police. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, marched in a demonstration on Tuesday and has expressed support for student protesters. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Protesters block a road in Nancy in north-eastern Frace in preparation for an afternoon rally. Photograph: Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu/Getty Images A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as ⁠the Avenue des Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations. About 100 people walked towards the police at the beginning protest yelling, “all cops are bastards!”. “We are fighting because the cost of living is ‌too harsh, because the price of ‌fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to ‌protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola. Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape. View image in fullscreen Police officers clash with protesters in Paris. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/AFP/Getty Images On Friday, the president appealed for calm and respect for people and property as officials warned of possible violence. “There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself, and I have always been vigilant and attentive that that right is fully respected,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.” Macron denounced as “unacceptable” the potential presence of people “solely to cause damage and create unrest”. View image in fullscreen A protester waves a French national flag during clashes before a demonstration in Marseille. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images Nuñez said hundreds of protest actions and more than 80 marches were expected nationwide, including spontaneous gatherings, street demonstrations and blockades. Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many Métro stations were closed on Saturday at the police’s request, including those around the Champs-Élysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices. View image in fullscreen Protesters vandalise a municipal police station in Marseille. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst Read more In recent weeks, there have been thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence, while the French prime minister said that more than 900 police officers had been injured. Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons . Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand, but said that they could be used on Saturday. On Tuesday, the climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
